title: Changes in Depreciation Estimates
description: Account for changes in useful life, residual value and other depreciation estimates.
html:
Accounting estimates can change

A company may later obtain new information showing that an asset's useful life or residual value differs from the original estimate.

A change in estimate is generally handled prospectively.

Prospectively means:

Do not go back and rewrite depreciation from previous periods simply because the estimate changed.

Instead, use the new estimate for the current and future periods.

Example

Equipment originally cost $50,000 with no residual value and a 5-year useful life.

Original Annual Depreciation = $50,000 ÷ 5 = $10,000

After two years, accumulated depreciation is $20,000.

Carrying Amount = $50,000 − $20,000 = $30,000

At that point, the company determines the asset will last four additional years.

New depreciation

$30,000 ÷ 4 remaining years = $7,500 per year

Notice what we did NOT do

We did not change the $10,000 depreciation recorded in either of the first two years.

The new information affects depreciation going forward.

General approach

  1. Determine current carrying amount.
  2. Determine the revised residual value, if applicable.
  3. Determine remaining useful life.
  4. Calculate depreciation for current and future periods.

quiz.prompt: An asset has a carrying amount of $36,000 when its remaining useful life is revised to 3 years with no residual value. What is annual straight-line depreciation going forward?
quiz.explanation: $36,000 ÷ 3 remaining years = $12,000 per year. The revised estimate is applied prospectively.
